title: Weight and plasma lipid control by decaffeinated green tea.
text_summary: 本文在瘦素缺陷ob/ob肥胖小鼠及其瘦型同窝小鼠中评估无咖啡因绿茶对体重和血脂的影响。小鼠随机饮用无咖啡因绿茶或缓冲液6周。绿茶从第1周起即减缓ob/ob小鼠体重增长，并降低其血浆胆固醇、甘油三酯和脂联素；瘦型小鼠体重无显著变化，粪便脂质也未明显改变。研究表明不依赖咖啡因的绿茶成分可能帮助肥胖状态下的体重和血脂控制，同时允许全天饮用而避免咖啡因兴奋作用，但其机制及人体适用性仍需进一步研究。

Weight and plasma lipid control by decaffeinated green tea
Doriane Richard a,∗ , Kaouthar Keﬁ a , Ullah Barbe a , Andrea Poli b , Pedro Bausero a , Francesco Visioli a
a

Laboratory of “Micronutrients and Cardiovascular Disease”, UR4, UPMC Univ 06, Paris, France

a r t i c l e

i n f o

Received 26 January 2009
Received in revised form 28 January 2009
Accepted 28 January 2009
Keywords:
Green tea
Obesity
Polyphenols
Diet
Decaffeinated

a b s t r a c t
We investigated whether regular decaffeinated green tea intake could modulate body weight in an experimental model of obesity. Male leptin-deﬁcient (ob/ob) mice and their C57BL/6J lean littermates (4 weeks
of age; n 20/genotype) were assigned randomly to receive either decaffeinated green tea or vehicle, for
6 weeks. Body weights were recorded weekly and ﬂuid intake was measured at each replacement. Blood
was collected from the heart into collection tubes, with Li+ -heparin as the anticoagulant. Administration
of decaffeinated green tea to ob/ob mice signiﬁcantly slowed their rate of weight gain, as compared with
animals that were fed buffer alone. This effect is apparent after only 1 week of supplementation. No
signiﬁcant difference was recorded between C57BL/6J lean mice administrated decaffeinated green tea
and those given buffer alone. Decaffeinated green tea consumption by ob/ob mice was also associated
with signiﬁcantly lower cholesterolemia, triglyceridemia, and adiponectin concentration. Fecal lipids did
not change signiﬁcantly throughout the experiment. In conclusion, administration of decaffeinated green
tea might contribute to weight control and provides an opportunity for through-the-day consumption,
without the excitatory effects of caffeine.

1. Introduction
The obesity epidemic increased markedly in the 1980s. Since the
late 1990s, the WHO and many national governments have recognized the importance of obesity as a major public-health problem
affecting both the developed and the developing world [1,2]. Obesity and its sequelae have profound socio-economic consequences
and represent a major contributor to the current global burden
of disease [3]. Therefore, preventive measures should be incorporated practice, including implementing of nutritional policies [4,5],
healthy lifestyle guidelines [6], and public-health initiatives [7].
Diet, along with genetic and environmental factors, is a major
factor affecting longevity as well as vascular disease outcome. There
is accumulating evidence that diets enriched in micronutrients,
including vitamins, minerals, and essential fatty acids maintain cellular antioxidant status and stress response enzyme activity, which
otherwise decrease with age and disease [8]. Green tea contains a
class of polyphenolic ﬂavonoids known as catechins, which include
epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), epicatechin gallate, and gallocatechin gallate. EGCG is thought to be the most pharmacologically
active of the catechins, and it is being studied in several models of
disease, including weight disorders [9].

Such studies utilize green tea extract [10] or pure EGCG [11],
whereas experimental approximation of real-life consumption
should employ brewed green tea. Further, the presence of both caffeine and ﬂavonoids in green tea makes it difﬁcult to disentangle
the metabolic effects of the two tea constituents. The availability
of decaffeinated green tea allows dissociation of the pharmacological effects of ﬂavonoids and caffeine. Therefore, we investigated
whether regular decaffeinated green tea intake could modulate
body weight in an experimental model of obesity.

2. Materials and methods
2.1. Animals and study design
The protocol for the care and use of animals was approved by
the Animal Care Committee at Université Pierre et Marie Curie.
Male leptin-deﬁcient (ob/ob) mice and their C57BL/6J lean littermates (4 weeks of age; n 20/genotype) were purchased from
Charles River (Paris, France). Mice were housed in a temperatureand humidity-controlled room with a 12-h light/dark cycle. All
mice were acclimated for 1 week prior to the experiment. Mice
(10 genotype−1 dietary treatment−1 ) were assigned randomly to
receive either a solution of 2% (w/v) decaffeinated green tea (kind
gift of Bonomelli s.p.a., Italy). This dose was shown to exert chemopreventive effects [12]. The tea was fully characterized in terms
of catechin composition. High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) analysis showed that this tea contains 71.75 mg total

catechins per g of leaves, of which 1.38 mg were catechin, 6.77 mg
were epicatechin, 4.45 mg were gallocatechin, 32.21 mg were epigallocatechin, 21.04 mg were epigallocatechin gallate, 0.39 mg were
gallocatechin gallate, 5.51 mg were epicatechin gallate, while catechin gallate was non-detectable. The tea was prepared by brewing
loose leaf tea (2 g/100 ml) for 3 min in just-boiled 0.5% citric acid
buffer (26 mM, pH 2.7, which enhances the stability of tea constituents compared with milliQ water alone [13]). Solutions were
prepared fresh every 3 days, and the stability of tea constituents
was veriﬁed by HPLC [13].
Body weights were recorded weekly and ﬂuid intake was measured at each replacement. Mice had free access to the diets
throughout the study. At the conclusion of the 6-week intervention,
mice were anesthetized with ketamine and xylazine. Blood was collected from the heart into collection tubes, with Li+ -heparin as the
anticoagulant. Plasma was obtained by centrifugation and stored at
−80 ◦ C.
2.2. Plasma lipids and adiponectin
Plasma total cholesterol and triacylglycerol concentrations were
analyzed by standard clinical assays (Sentinel, Milan, Italy; kits
number 17644 and 17624, respectively), in accordance with the
manufacturer’s instructions. Plasma adiponectin concentration
was measured by ELISA (Cayman Inalco, Milan, Italy).
2.3. Fecal lipids
Fecal samples were collected before and at the end of the study.
Feces were extracted with choloroform:methanol (2:1, v/v) [14],
and total fat was quantiﬁed by microgravimetry.
Fig. 1. Weekly body weight of obese (ob/ob; panel A) and lean (C57BL/6J; panel
B) mice administered decaffeinated green tea, ad libitum for 6 weeks. Values are
means ± S.D., n = 10. *p < 0.05.

2.4. Statistical analysis
Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism (Version 4.03; GraphPad Software). Data are expressed as means ± S.D.
Comparisons between treatments (tea vs. vehicle) were done by
Student’s t-test.
3. Results
Administration of decaffeinated green tea to ob/ob mice signiﬁcantly slowed their rate of weight gain, as compared with animals
that were fed buffer alone (Fig. 1, panel A). This effect is apparent
after only 1 week of supplementation. No signiﬁcant difference was
recorded between C57BL/6J lean mice administrated decaffeinated
green tea and those given buffer alone (Fig. 1, panel B).
Concerning plasma lipids, no difference was observed between
treatments of C57BL/6J lean mice. Conversely, decaffeinated green
tea consumption by ob/ob mice was associated with signiﬁcantly
lower cholesterolemia, triglyceridemia, and adiponectin concentration (Table 1).
Fecal lipids did not change quantitatively throughout the experiment (neither after tea nor after water administration) and
exhibited a high variability (Table 1).

4. Discussion
In this study, we report that administration of decaffeinated
green tea to genetically obese mice (ob/ob) signiﬁcantly slows their
weight gain. The same effect was not observed in their C57BL/6J lean
littermates. Lower rate of weight gain was associated with lower
concentrations of plasma adiponectin, cholesterol, and triglycerides.
Adiponectin plays an important role in the regulation of insulin
function and energy homeostasis and negatively correlates with
several cardiovascular risk factors [15]. In agreement with Bruno
et al. [16] we found that adiponectin concentrations were not elevated by green tea administration to ob/ob mice. Thus, the effects of
decaffeinated green tea are unlikely to be mediated by adiponectin
pathways. While this apparent discrepancy requires further investigation, one potential explanation is that leptin is needed to restore
plasma adiponectin in ob/ob mice [17].
The effects of decaffeinated green tea on plasma lipids, namely
cholesterol and triacylglycerols, conﬁrm previous reports [9,18],
though it was only observed in genetically obese animals. By

using decaffeinated green tea administered as drinking ﬂuid –
thereby approximating human consumption – we were able to
distinguish the effects of tea catechins (previously only administered as extracts) from those of caffeine. Caffeine inhibits
the phosphodiesterase-induced degradation of intracellular cyclic
AMP, a critical intracellular mediator for the action of catecholamines on thermogenesis. Indeed, green tea has been shown
to reduce body weight in healthy [19] and obese subjects [20] by
increasing energy expenditure and fat oxidation. This effect might
be also mediated by caffeine [21], although in vitro and animal data
attribute catechins with similar abilities [22,23]. Furthermore, catechins are considered as ligands of nuclear transcription factors,
particularly PPARs [24]. As PPAR gamma are highly expressed in
adipocytes and regulate the transcription of genes involved in lipid
metabolism, they might represent a molecular target of green tea
components.
Tea catechins have been suggested to reduce plasma cholesterol and hypertriglycerydemia by reducing triglyceride absorption,
although the mechanisms of these reductions are not yet clear. A
possible explanation is that tea polyphenols may modify dietary fat
emulsiﬁcation in the gastrointestinal tract [25]. In particular, green
tea components (i.e. catechins) might affect lipid metabolism by
interfering with the micellar solubilization of cholesterol in the
digestive tract, which, in turn, decreases cholesterol absorption
[26]. At the “Tea and Health” symposium that took place at the
ICPH2007 meeting, the hypothesis was formulated (C.S. Yang, personal communication) that green tea catechin might bind dietary
lipids, favoring their fecal excretion thus limiting their absorption, as shown with oolong [27] and green [28] teas. Indeed,
there is evidence that green tea inhibits intestinal lipid absorption [28–30], though this hypothesis has never been tested in
ob/ob mice and, to our knowledge, never on fecal lipid content.
Hence, we veriﬁed this assumption by quantifying total fecal lipids
by microgravimetry. Our results (Table 1) point to that direction, even though a high interindividual variability was recorded
and might have masked a signiﬁcant effect. On the other hand,
Fiorini et al. [31] showed that oral or intraperitoneal administration of EGCG in ob/ob mice decreased hepatic steatosis, which
was accompanied by decreased hepatic de novo lipogenesis. In
turn, a combination of effects – rather than a single mechanism
– is likely responsible for the observed effects of green tea on
weight.
In our study, it should be noted that we did not control for
food intake. Hence, we cannot exclude a direct, anorectic effect of
decaffeinated green tea and its components, as suggested by Kao
et al. [32]. However, Bruno et al. reported that food intakes were
not affected by genotype or green tea extract treatment throughout their study on ob/ob and C57BL/6J mice [16]; it is noteworthy
that the catechins doses we administered were much lower than
those of Bruno et al. (who employed a green tea extract). In turn,
the issue of an anorectic effect of green tea remains unresolved.
One other limitation of the current study is that it was stopped
after six weeks. Hence, we cannot exclude neither that the effects
of decaffeinated green tea taper off after this period nor that a slight
weight-gaining effect be noted in wild-type mice (as suggested by
data in Fig. 1).
The major advantage of decaffeinated green tea in helping control weight gain in obesity is that it provides an opportunity for
through-the-day consumption, without the excitatory effects of
caffeine. Hence, consumption of higher amounts, with respect to
regular green tea, is feasible and might become integral part of a
dietary regimen in obese subjects. However, our results must ﬁrst
be conﬁrmed in humans, as differences in energy expenditure have
been recorded between rodents and humans; in addition, it should
be underlined that our results were obtained by administering
decaffeinated green tea as the sole drinking ﬂuid.

353

In conclusion, administration of green tea (either regular or
decaffeinated for caffeine-sensitive subjects), in addition to appropriate life style management and pharmacological therapy, might
contribute to the treatment of obesity.

第2页：说明血脂、脂联素、粪便脂质及统计方法；结果和Figure 1显示绿茶减缓肥胖小鼠增重，表1列出血浆与粪便指标，并开始讨论。
第3页：讨论茶儿茶素、脂质吸收、体重和脂联素变化的可能机制及人体意义，包含致谢和参考文献。
第4页：继续并结束参考文献。
